title: Hoverboard: safe teardown
summary: A hoverboard gives two brushless hub motors in their wheels, a 36 V lithium-ion pack of about 20 cells, a motor controller board, gyro boards, LEDs and a 42 V charger. The pack is the danger: hoverboard packs have overheated and caught fire, some while charging. Check it before you charge or open anything, and keep the pack whole.

steps.text: Before you charge it or open it, make sure it is switched off (lights out), then take it outdoors and look it over in daylight. Don't lift or tip a board that is switched on: Jetson says its wheels spin when it is lifted off the ground while on. Check the shell for cracks, bulges, scorch marks or melted plastic, sniff for a sweet chemical smell, and feel the middle of the board for heat. If you find any of these, stop and follow safety_swollen_lithium with the whole board.
steps.warn: Never charge a hoverboard with a cracked, swollen, wet or damaged case. Hoverboard packs have overheated, smoked and caught fire (CPSC 16-218), some while charging (iFixit Swagway).

steps.text: Turn it over and look at the bottom for a UL certification label: CPSC says a UL 2272 compliant board carries a holographic one with the Enhanced Mark there. Boards bought before 29 January 2016 are not UL 2272 compliant (CPSC hoverboard alert). A board with no such label, or one from before that date, fails this check. About 501,000 boards from 10 firms, sold June 2015 to May 2016, were recalled for fire (CPSC 16-218). Brands in that recall include Swagway X1, Razor Hovertrax, iMoto, Powerboard, Hype Roam and Hover-Way. Razor recalled GLW battery packs sold with Hovertrax 2.0 boards in 2021 (CPSC micromobility). The 42-volt Jetson Rogue made in 2018–2019 was recalled too; it has a three-pin charge port to the left of the power button (CPSC 23-165). Don't charge any of these: go straight on to the teardown and keep the pack whole.

If it passed both checks, you know it was working when it was put away, and you want it running, charge it with its own charger only, with the board switched off (Jetson Plasma X manual), on concrete or stone, away from anything that burns, and stay with it. Unplug it if the board gets warm, and never charge it overnight or while you sleep (CPSC hoverboard alert, CPSC micromobility, Jetson Plasma X manual). If you don't know how it was stored, or it has sat flat for a long time, skip charging: open it and measure the pack first (safety_swollen_lithium).
steps.warn: Charge only between 0 and 40 °C (32–104 °F) (Jetson Plasma X manual). Charging lithium cells below freezing damages them (OSHA SHIB 06-20-2019).

steps.text: Switch it off, unplug the charger, and lay the board upside down on a blanket or cardboard. Undo every screw in the bottom shell: the Titan has 8 per half; the H1 has 22, plus 2 hidden under black stickers (iFixit Titan battery, iFixit H1 battery). Lift each half slowly. If a half sticks, don't push a screwdriver or blade into the seam: the pack sits just inside. Look for a missed screw, or use a plastic opener only.
steps.warn: Wires run from the shell to the lights, speaker, charge port and power button. Lift gently so you don't tear them off their plugs (iFixit H1 battery).

steps.text: Find the battery: a long block on one side, with the main board on the other (iFixit Swagway). Unplug it first, gripping the connector body, never the wires: orange on the Hover-1 H1, yellow on the Titan, black and yellow on the Razor Hovertrax 2.0 (iFixit H1 battery, iFixit Titan battery, iFixit Razor hub). Tape over both halves of the plug.
steps.warn: Keep metal tools off the pack's connector pins. A short across a 36 V pack can weld a tool, burn you and start a fire.

steps.text: Look at the pack now you can see it. A swollen, dented or split case, a leak, heat or a sweet smell means stop and follow safety_swollen_lithium. If it is sound, undo its fixings (four screws on the H1 and Titan, two hex bolts on the Razor) and lift it out by its case (iFixit H1 battery, iFixit Titan battery, iFixit Razor hub).
steps.warn: Keep the pack whole. Don't cut its wrap, open it or pull cells out: the Titan manual says never to open the battery or put anything into it (Hover-1 Titan manual).

steps.text: Wait 5 minutes with the battery out. The Razor guide warns that a capacitor under its board may still hold a charge (iFixit Razor hub). Bridge the largest capacitor's leads with a resistor tool (see safety_discharge_capacitor), then check it with a meter you have just tried on a known battery: it must read under 1 V. Check the meter on that battery again afterwards, and leave a wire across the capacitor's leads while you work. Handle the board by its edges.

Photograph the wiring. Then unplug each motor from the main board: three thick phase wires and a five-wire Hall sensor plug per motor (iFixit Swagway, Fictiv hoverboard). On the Titan the yellow, green and blue wire plugs sit inside rubber that has to be cut open: use scissors or a knife, cutting away from you (the guide lists both tools and doesn't say which cuts the rubber; iFixit Titan wheel). Tape over every lead you unplug and keep the wheels still: a hub motor makes voltage when its wheel turns, and a fast-spinning wheel can make a dangerous amount (Fictiv hoverboard, ODrive hoverboard).

Undo the main board's screws and lift it out with its metal plate. Then take the gyro boards (one on each side in the Swagway), the foot-pad sensors, the LED boards, the speaker, the charge port and the power switch (iFixit Swagway, Fictiv hoverboard).

Remove each wheel: undo the bolts in the clamp plate over the axle, lift the plate off, feed the wires through, and lift the wheel and axle out (iFixit Titan wheel, iFixit Maverick wheel, iFixit Razor hub). The Titan uses four 20 mm hex bolts; the Razor uses four 22 mm hex bolts plus two smaller bolts that take a 10 mm socket (iFixit Titan wheel, iFixit Razor hub).
steps.warn: The Razor guide says its bolts need force to undo (iFixit Razor hub). Brace the board so it can't slip, and wear safety glasses if you use an impact driver (iFixit Titan wheel). Each wheel weighed about 5.4 kg (12 lb) in one teardown (Fictiv hoverboard).

steps.text: Leave the hub motors closed unless you need their magnets. Each wheel is a sealed motor with its tyre, axle and bearings, and is most useful whole.

Open a hub only if you need its magnets, with the wheel off the board and every motor lead taped. The method below is from a guide for e-bike hub motors (Grin hub motor); no hoverboard source confirms it, so check that your hub has screwed side covers and stop if it hasn't. Take the nuts and washers off the axle and undo the side-cover screws on the wire side. Put a gear puller on the other side, legs under the hub flange and centre on the axle, and turn it slowly so the axle pushes the stator out. Let the stator drop onto something soft (Grin hub motor).
steps.warn: Strong magnets can slam the stator back into the rotor and take fingers with it. Keep hands clear and let it drop, don't pull it (Grin hub motor). Wear glasses and gloves. Keep magnets from pacemakers and children.

steps.text: Unbolt the two frame halves if you want the cast aluminium and the hollow steel centre shaft (Fictiv hoverboard).

Store the pack part-charged, with its plug taped, on concrete or in a metal box of dry sand with a loose lid, away from where people sleep. Check it often for heat or swelling (OSHA SHIB 06-20-2019, safety_swollen_lithium).

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The whole board, if it runs.** The two motors and the main board together can drive a cart or a slow platform. Open-source firmware exists for the common single-mainboard type with an STM32F103RCT6 or GD32F103RCT6 chip; its README links a wheelchair project and a hoverboard-based transport system, and recommends one of its modes for robotics (EFeru FOC firmware). You need a programmer and a saved copy of the firmware. Don't power the board from the programmer's 3.3 V: that has destroyed boards (NiklasFauth firmware).
- **Battery pack.** The Swagway X1 pack was labelled 36 V, 4.4 Ah (158 Wh) and held 20 LG 18650 cells and a protection board with four MOSFETs (iFixit Swagway). The Hover-1 Titan manual lists 36 V, 4 Ah, 20 cells (Hover-1 Titan manual); the Jetson Plasma X lists 36 V, 2.0 Ah (Jetson Plasma X manual). A 36 V lithium-ion pack is 10 cells in series, full at 42 V, which matches the Swagway's 42 V charger (iFixit Swagway). Reuse a pack only if it is undamaged and not from a recalled board or one bought before 29 January 2016 (see What to leave). Use it whole, with its protection board and a fuse at its output: it runs 36 V motors and lights, or a 12 V system through a DC-DC converter rated for 42 V input. Charge it only with its own charger.
- **Hub motors.** Brushless three-phase motors inside the wheels, each with three thick phase wires and five thin Hall sensor wires (iFixit Swagway, Fictiv hoverboard). The common 6.5 inch motor has 30 magnet poles, and its Hall sensors run on 5 V (ODrive hoverboard). With a brushless controller they move carts. Spun by hand, water or wind they give three-phase AC; a bridge rectifier turns it into DC. ODrive's guide gives 16 as a typical KV value for these motors but doesn't state its units. If it is rpm per volt, the usual unit, a wheel at about 500 rpm could give around 30 V, so insulate the leads and treat a fast-spinning wheel as live; measure your own motor (ODrive hoverboard).
- **Main board.** The Swagway's board has a GigaDevice GD32F103 microcontroller, six half-bridge drivers and 12 large MOSFETs on a metal plate, plus current-sense resistors that let it stop a stalled motor (iFixit Swagway). Keep it with its motors. Its MOSFETs and plate are good spares.
- **Gyro boards and foot sensors.** Each Swagway gyro board carries an MPU-6050 gyro and accelerometer and a small GD32F130 microcontroller. Each foot pad has two infrared sensors, toe and heel (iFixit Swagway). Use them as tilt sensors and beam-break sensors.
- **Charger.** The Swagway's charger was 42 V, 2 A, a well-isolated switch-mode supply (iFixit Swagway). Keep it with its pack: it suits only 10-cell lithium-ion packs. Don't open it: it is a mains device.
- **LEDs, speaker, switch and charge port.** Small spares. The Titan and the Plasma X have built-in Bluetooth speakers (Hover-1 Titan manual, Jetson Plasma X manual).
- **Frame.** Two cast aluminium halves joined by a hollow steel shaft that carries the wiring (Fictiv hoverboard).

## Variations

- **Pack size:** 4.4 Ah (Swagway), 4 Ah (Titan), 2.0 Ah (Plasma X). Read the label on yours; don't assume 36 V.
- **Boards:** a single main board with two gyro side boards, or split boards (EFeru FOC firmware). The Maverick has one motherboard on each side near the wheels (iFixit Maverick wheel).
- **Fixings:** the battery is held by four screws (H1, Titan) or two hex bolts (Razor); the battery plug is orange, yellow, or black and yellow (iFixit H1 battery, iFixit Titan battery, iFixit Razor hub).
- **Wheel bolts:** the Titan has four 20 mm hex bolts in a clamp plate over the axle; the Maverick has four 15 mm hex screws holding a metal cover over the motor; the Razor has four 22 mm hex bolts plus two smaller bolts that take a 10 mm socket (iFixit Titan wheel, iFixit Maverick wheel, iFixit Razor hub).

## Why the pack matters

- In 2016, about 501,000 hoverboards from 10 firms were recalled after at least 99 reports of packs overheating, sparking, smoking, catching fire or exploding, with burns and property damage (CPSC 16-218).
- By late 2017 CPSC knew of more than 250 hoverboard fire or overheating incidents. Two girls died in a 2017 house fire in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, started by a hoverboard (CPSC hoverboard alert).
- In 2023 about 53,000 Jetson Rogue boards were recalled. Two sisters died in a 2022 house fire in Hellertown, Pennsylvania; the fire marshal found a Rogue at the point of origin, though the cause is undetermined (CPSC 23-165).
- Even a UL 2272 board can overheat or catch fire (CPSC hoverboard alert). CPSC says many lithium-ion home fires and deaths happened at night, while batteries charged and families slept (CPSC micromobility).
- Heat above 54 °C (130 °F), dropping, crushing and puncturing all damage lithium cells. Bulging, cracking, hissing, leaking, rising heat or smoke mean move the pack away from anything that burns, then into a metal container with sand (OSHA SHIB 06-20-2019).
- Don't put a hoverboard pack in household rubbish or shop battery bins (CPSC 23-165, CPSC micromobility).

## What to leave

- **Damaged, recalled or pre-2016 packs.** Store them whole in sand, outdoors, and never charge them (safety_swollen_lithium). CPSC says not to donate or resell a recalled Jetson Rogue, and to take a recalled pack to a battery recycler or hazardous-waste collection point, not to the rubbish or a shop battery bin; use these where they still work (CPSC 23-165, CPSC micromobility).
- **The inside of the pack.** Use it whole.
- **The inside of the hub motors,** unless you need the magnets.
- **The inside of the charger.** It is a mains supply.
- **Plastic shells and rubber foot mats,** unless you need them.

## Testing what you got out

- **Pack:** set the meter to DC volts with the red lead in the volts socket (never the amps socket, which makes a dead short across the pack), and keep the probe tips apart. Measure at its plug. A 10-cell pack reads about 30–42 V. Much lower means flat or failing cells. Below about 20 V (2 V a cell) don't charge it (safety_swollen_lithium).
- **Hub motor:** spin the wheel by hand with the meter on AC volts across any two of the three thick wires. A good motor gives a small voltage that rises with speed, about the same on all three pairs (see test_motor).
- **Board and sensors:** easiest to test together, with the motors and pack connected as they came out.
